title: Inverse demand function

definition.text: A formula that gives price as a function of the quantity demanded, so it is also called a price function.

facts.text: Its value is the highest price that could be charged while still selling that quantity; it equals the average revenue function.
It is found by solving the demand function for price: if Q = 240 − 2P, then P = 120 − Q/2.
For a straight-line demand P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is MR = a − 2bQ: the same starting height and twice the slope.
It is used to find the profit-maximising output, where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and then the price to charge.

notes: Sentence afe171025897 renders the inverse as 'P=120−12Q', a lost fraction (1/2 Q); the fact paraphrases it as Q/2, which is what 240 − 2P solved for P gives and what the TR line e9be0558cc94 implies. Verify.

title: Invisible hand

definition.text: Adam Smith's metaphor for the way free markets can lead self-interested people to serve the public good without meaning to.

facts.text: Smith used the phrase only once each in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) and The Wealth of Nations, and spoke of 'an' invisible hand, never 'the'.
In The Wealth of Nations it appears in a chapter about where merchants invest their capital, not about free trade.
Paul Samuelson's 1948 textbook popularised the phrase and gave it a new meaning: that free markets regulate themselves and reach outcomes government cannot improve.
The idea that market exchange channels self-interest toward social good is a central justification for laissez-faire thinking behind neoclassical economics.
Joseph Stiglitz argues the hand often seems invisible because it is not there: with externalities, markets on their own produce too much pollution.
Environmental economics deals largely with market failures, where the invisible hand is unreliable.

contested_note: Economists such as Stiglitz and Piketty argue that markets often fail to turn self-interest into social good, and scholars disagree about what Smith himself meant.

definition.text: The basic rule that, all else being equal, people buy less of a good when its price rises and more when it falls.

facts.text: It says only which way quantity moves when price changes, not by how much.
It is drawn as the demand curve, with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical, which slopes downward.
A price change moves buyers along the demand curve; changes in the number of buyers, income, tastes, prices of related goods or expectations shift the whole curve.
Charles Davenant first stated it in 1699, and Alfred Marshall drew it as a graph and joined it with supply in his Principles of Economics (1890).
Together with the law of supply, it fixes the equilibrium price and quantity.
Exceptions include Giffen goods, Veblen goods, necessities and cases where buyers expect prices to keep changing.

title: Giffen good

definition.text: An inferior good that people buy more of when its price rises, against the law of demand.

facts.text: Potatoes in the Irish Great Famine are a classic example: as their price rose, people cut back on meat and vegetables and bought more potatoes.
Economists disagree about whether Giffen goods actually exist in real markets.

contested_note: Economists disagree on whether Giffen goods exist in real markets.

definition.text: A luxury good whose demand rises as its price rises, because a high price signals status.

facts.text: Examples include diamonds, gold, precious stones, famous paintings and antiques.
Thorstein Veblen described such buying as paying for status and social position rather than extra usefulness.

title: Law of supply

definition.text: The basic rule that, all else being equal, a higher price leads sellers to offer more of a good.

facts.text: Producers offer more at higher prices because producing more is a way to make more profit; this is why the supply curve slopes upward.
A job paying £20 an hour draws more interest than one paying £15 an hour.
Things other than price shift the supply curve: production costs, the number of suppliers, subsidies, taxes and, in farming, the weather.
If buyers want more than sellers offer, the price rises, cutting demand and raising supply until the two match.
Some heterodox economists, such as Steve Keen, argue the supply curve for mass-produced goods often slopes downward.

contested_note: Some heterodox economists dispute the law of supply for mass-produced goods, whose unit prices may fall as output grows.
